summary:
We developed an interactive web-based astronomical analysis tool that queries NASA SPHEREx spectral image data and visualizes proper motion and transient objects across multiple observational passes. Addressing the challenge of identifying moving celestial targets within large infrared survey datasets, our application fetches real-time FITS cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA and AWS S3 archives by sky coordinates (ICRS/Galactic) and performs automated Moving Target Indication (MTI).

Users can sequentially step through chronological observational passes, generate median-subtracted difference images, and inspect signal-to-noise significance alongside interactive Aladin Lite sky overlays. By transforming raw multi-wavelength FITS arrays into immediate visual comparisons, the tool lowers the barrier for researchers, citizen scientists, and educators to detect fast-moving stars (such as Barnard’s Star and Kapteyn’s Star), asteroids, and transient phenomena without requiring complex local astronomical software pipelines.
details:
Obelix – Understand Space Through Obelix is a browser tool that finds and characterises moving objects in data from NASA’s SPHEREx all sky survey.

What it does and how it works. SPHEREx images the whole sky in 102 infrared colours (0.75–5 µm) every six months, and there are already more than a million image files. You enter coordinates or a target name, and Obelix narrows the search in steps:

  1. The Sun’s position tells it in which weeks SPHEREx could see the target (151 → 42 week folders).
  2. A 16 KB read of each file header shows which pointings can contain it (28,575 → 305).
  3. An exact footprint check keeps only images that really contain the target (449,845 files → 239 for Barnard’s Star).
  4. From each of those images, only a 100 × 100 pixel cutout is read.

Then it reduces the data in two ways:

  • Tracking: align all exposures north-up, remove the sky background, mask bad pixels, combine each pass into one image and subtract the passes from each other. Whatever moved appears as a dark and a bright spot, and fitting the positions over time gives the proper motion. For Barnard’s Star we measured 10.35″ per year; Gaia gives 10.4″.
  • Classification: measure the brightness in every colour and compare the spectral shape with reference profiles of F to M dwarfs (Pecaut & Mamajek), plus a methane test at 3.3/4.6 µm. The result is yellow dwarf, red dwarf, methane atmosphere, or “not classifiable”. Objects SPHEREx cannot detect, such as neutron stars or super-Earths, are reported honestly instead of guessed.

Benefits and impact. Anyone can work with SPHEREx data in a browser, without a supercomputer or downloading terabytes. Obelix reads well under 1 % of the data and gets the same images. It is a first step towards searching the whole sky for faint, slow movers such as a possible Planet X, and towards listing red dwarfs as targets for habitable-planet searches.

Creativity and robustness. When NASA’s IRSA archive search returned HTTP 502 errors during the hackathon, we built our own search directly on NASA’s open SPHEREx data on AWS. It uses orbit geometry and header-only range reads, so Obelix keeps working even when the archive is down. Results are cached, so a repeat search skips the downloads.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, Astropy, astroquery, pyvo, pandas, Pillow, s3fs/fsspec, requests); HTML/CSS/JavaScript with Aladin Lite; NASA IRSA APIs and the AWS S3 bucket nasa-irsa-spherex; SIMBAD for names and proper motions; Windows laptops; GitHub.

Factors we considered. Data volume and speed, archive outages, honest physical limits (no invented thresholds; every limit is derived from published colours and SPHEREx sensitivity), clear labelling of simulated demo data versus real measurements, and accessibility for non-experts.
